new_statements.citation: Havens, Emily Paige. 2024. A Phonological Sketch of Ciacia, with Implications for Orthography. MA thesis, Dallas International University. §5.3 Stress Assignment.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (125 pp., text layer; printed page = PDF page - 15). §5.3 "Stress Assignment" begins on printed p. 60 (PDF p. 75). The quoted passage is there word for word: "Stress in Ciacia is primarily marked by higher pitch, but stressed syllables also tend to be longer in duration and higher in intensity than unstressed syllables. Primary stress is predictably found on the penultimate syllable of Ciacia words. Each vowel is in its own syllable. Neither the weight of the syllable nor affixation affects stress placement. As (34) shows, no matter the weight of the syllables in the word, the stress falls on the penultimate syllable." Printed p. 61 (PDF p. 76): "Stress is applied to the full affixed…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the whole (affixed) phonological word; every vowel counts as a syllable (so siua 'nine' is [si.ˈu.a]); syllable weight plays no role; suffixes shift stress rightward (ŋeaaso [ŋẽ.ã.ˈʔa.so] vs niŋeaasono [ni.ŋẽ.ã.ʔa.ˈso.no]). Stress is cued chiefly by higher F0, secondarily by duration and intensity. Independently corroborated by van den Berg 1991: 311 ('invariably recorded on the penultimate syllable') and Mead & Truong 2021: 60 ('Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable'); Abdullah et al. 1991: 23 add that stress and pitch are not contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Havens 2024: 62: 'Secondary stress is not as predictable as primary stress. If there is a discernible pattern of increased pitch, volume, and duration, it is minimal.' Mead & Truong 2021: 61 (rules illustrated with Lasalimu but said to apply across the data set): secondary stress usually on the fourth-from-last syllable; in two-syllable reduplications the first syllable of the reduplicant takes it (kamia-mia [kaˌmiaˈmia], limba-limbaʔa [ˌlimbaliˈmbaʔa]).
new_statements.exceptions: Havens 2024: 64-65: optional elision of the [o] of perfective -mo does not move stress, yielding surface final stress ([mobuˈntʃimo] ~ [mobuˈntʃim]). van den Berg 1991: 311: the trisyllabic haeo 'charcoal' has antepenultimate stress; dialect-B apocope of o/u after m (mbulem < mbule-mo) is ordered after stress assignment; siua 'nine' (antepenult in Muna) is regular penult in Cia-Cia. Mead & Truong 2021: 61: a few unpredictable cases are marked in the word lists.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the entire affixed phonological word in citation/elicited forms (Praat pitch traces of wordlist items); Havens describes the Bahari-village variety (central-eastern dialect); van den Berg's speakers were from Lapandewa (Sampolawa) and Gonda (Pasarwajo).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog ciac1237 (ISO cia), no dialect subdivisions. Havens 2024 describes the variety of the three Bahari villages (Pasarwajo area; central-eastern dialect in Mead & Truong's 2021 scheme; Bahari settlers came from Burangasi). van den Berg 1991 is based on two speakers from Lapandewa (kec. Sampolawa) and Gonda (kec. Pasarwajo), his dialects A and B. Mead & Truong 2021 state their stress rules with Lasalimu data (a separate language in Glottolog) but say they hold across all southern-Buton lects surveyed. Abdullah et al. 1991 worked mainly in the Pasarwajo area. Not the Binongko 'Island Cia-Cia' (Wali) variety. All three primary sources agree on penultimate stress, so the statement is not dialect-restricted in any way the sources note.

sources.note: §5.3 Stress Assignment, pp. 60-62: primary stress predictably on the penultimate syllable of the whole affixed phonological word, marked mainly by higher pitch (Praat traces); each vowel is its own syllable; syllable weight and affixation do not affect placement; siua 'nine' is regular [si.'u.a]; secondary stress minimal/unpredictable; optional elision of final [o] of -mo leaves stress in place ([poʔoˈlim]). Variety: Bahari villages.

sources.note: §3.4 Ciri Prosodi, p. 23: 'Tekanan dan nada dalam bahasa Cia-cia bukan merupakan fonem prosodi karena tidak dapat membedakan arti. Yang dianggap sebagai fonem prosodi dalam bahasa Cia-cia hanyalah pemanjangan, terutama yang terdapat pada bunyi-bunyi vokal.' (Stress and pitch are not prosodic phonemes because they cannot distinguish meaning; only length, chiefly of vowels, is.) No placement rule stated.
